title: Jazz Fest Began in a Square With a Much Older Story
description:
The Jazz Fest lineup is in the news this week. The very first New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, in 1970, drew about 350 people, and it was held in a park with a much older story: Congo Square.
🚶 Visiting San Diego? Explore its history on a guided tour with Fable: https://fablehospitality.com

Every frame is drawn with code. No stock footage, no AI video.

0:00 The first Jazz Fest, 1970
0:08 Congo Square, New Orleans
0:12 1724: Sundays off under the Code Noir
0:17 Sunday afternoons at the edge of town
0:23 1817: one place only
0:28 1819: Benjamin Latrobe's visit
0:34 "Two drums and a stringed instrument"
0:39 The bamboula
0:43 Shut down before the Civil War
0:46 1893: renamed Beauregard Square
0:51 One root of jazz
0:55 1970: Jazz Fest begins here
1:02 2011: Congo Square again

Note: Louisiana's Code Noir (Versailles, March 1724) made Sundays and holy days days without work, even for enslaved people. An 1817 city ordinance limited these Sunday gatherings to one place, which became known as Congo Square. Benjamin Henry Latrobe wrote in his journal (February 1819) that he found "five or six hundred persons" there, dancing in circular groups to "two drums and a stringed instrument", which he believed "no doubt was imported from Africa". The city shut the gatherings down more than once before the Civil War (sources give 1835 and 1851; they had faded by the 1850s). The square was renamed for P. G. T. Beauregard in 1893, and the City Council made the name Congo Square official in 2011. How directly Congo Square leads to jazz is debated; many historians see it as one root. The first Jazz & Heritage Festival (April 1970, Congo Square, then Beauregard Square) drew about 350 people, with Mahalia Jackson and Duke Ellington on the bill. E. W. Kemble's drawings were made for George W. Cable's 1886 article, decades after the dances ended.

Images (public domain): E. W. Kemble, "The Bamboula" and "A Congo Woman", from George W. Cable, "The Dance in Place Congo", The Century Magazine, February 1886 (Internet Archive); Le Code Noir ou Edit du Roy (1727 printing of the March 1724 Louisiana edict, John Carter Brown Library, via Internet Archive); portrait of B. H. Latrobe from The Journal of Latrobe (1905, Internet Archive); portrait of G. T. Beauregard from Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, vol. 1 (1887, Internet Archive). Documents drawn in code.
Maps drawn in code from Natural Earth (world-atlas) and US Census (us-atlas) outlines.
Narration voice is synthetic.
